This is expressed mathematically as a mapping between expected and actual goal states, \( \mathcal{E}(G_{\text{expected}}) \leftrightarrow \mathcal{D}(G_{\text{actual}}) \). The disruption is quantified via information-theoretic surprise, \( S = \log \frac{P(G_{\text{observed}})}{P(G_{\text{expected}})} \). Directional asymmetry arises because disruptions are more pronounced when moving from higher to lower demand goals, i.e., \( D_{\text{downward}} > D_{\text{upward}} \). This asymmetry reflects evolutionary optimization toward avoiding suboptimal outcomes. Latent surprise detection suggests that while overt disruption is absent in reverse-direction changes, subtle behavioral accelerations or timing shifts may still signal internal surprise, captured by \( \Delta t_{\text{behavior}} \). These primitives form a layered model where the first layer encodes expectation, the second encodes asymmetry, and the third models hidden behavioral signals.
